\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P2-CHEM-S1-Q01, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=2, qno=1, type=single, subtopic={Gas laws}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: liquid range of gallium and thermodynamic data | steps: boiling and melting difference; heat to raise and vaporise; compute asked}]
The element gallium (Ga) has the second largest liquid range of any element, melting at 29.78$^\circ$C and boiling at 2204$^\circ$C at atmospheric pressure.

Assume that you construct a thermometer using, gallium as the fluid instead of mercury, and that you define the melting point of gallium as 0$^\circ$G and the boiling point of gallium as 1000$^\circ$G. What is the melting point of sodium chloride (801$^\circ$C) on the gallium scale ?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{801}
\opt{B}{368}
\opt{C}{771.2}
\opt{D}{354.7}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

Consider a 1.0-L container of neon gas initially at STP. Will the average kinetic energy and frequency of collisions of gas molecules with the walls of the container increase, decrease, or remain the same under each of the following conditions?
\begin{center}\small\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\begin{tabular}{|c|p{3.4cm}|c|p{2.5cm}|}
\hline
\multicolumn{2}{|c|}{List-I} & \multicolumn{2}{c|}{List-II}\\ \hline
(P) & The temperature is increased to 100$^\circ$C. (at constant V) & (1) & Average Kinetic Energy Per mol Increase\\ \hline
(Q) & The temperature is decreased to $-50^\circ$C. (at constant V) & (2) & Same Average Kinetic Energy Per mol\\ \hline
(R) & The volume is decreased to 0.5 L. (at constant T) & (3) & wall collision frequency increase\\ \hline
(S) & The number of moles of neon is doubled. (at constant T and V) & (4) & wall collision frequency decrease\\ \hline
 & & (5) & Average Kinetic Energy Per mol decrease\\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\opt{C}{P $\to$ 1,4;Q $\to$ 2,3;R $\to$ 4,5;S $\to$ 3,5}
\opt{D}{P $\to$ 1,3;Q $\to$ 1,4;R $\to$ 1,4;S $\to$ 2,5}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI08-P2-CHEM-S4-Q07, source={Score-I - Test 08 (09 Feb 2022)}, paper=2, qno=7, type=numerical, subtopic={Real gases}, answer={100}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: temperature at which second virial coefficient vanishes or its value | steps: B(T) given empirically; Boyle temperature where B = 0; solve exponential equation}]
The second virial coefficient of methane can be approximate by the empirical equation :

$B=a+b\cdot e^{-c/T^2}$

where $a=-0.2\ \mathrm{bar^{-1}}$, $b=0.22\ \mathrm{bar^{-1}}$, and $c=950\ \mathrm{K^2}$. What is the value of the Boyle temperature of methane (in K)? ($\ln 1.1=0.095$)
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI31-P1-CHEM-S1-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 31 (29 Dec 2022)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=multi, subtopic={Real gases}, answer={A,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K1 S3 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: compressibility curve for hydrogen at low temperature from the van der Waals form | steps: Z = V/(V - b) - a/(V R T); at low pressure attraction dominates so Z less than 1; at high pressure repulsion dominates; identify the terms on the curve; check each | I: which of the two terms dominates in each pressure range}]
The Vander waal's equation of state for a non-ideal gas can be rearranged to give $\dfrac{PV}{RT}=\dfrac{V}{V-b}-\dfrac{a}{VRT}$ for 1 mole of gas. The constants $a$ \& $b$ are positive numbers. When applied to H$_2$ at 80 K, the equation gives the curve as shown in figure. Which one of the following statements is(are) correct?
\bfig{88.4}{SI31_p1_chem_s1_q02_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The two terms $\dfrac{V}{(V-b)}$ and $\dfrac{a}{VRT}$ are never equal}
\opt{B}{At 80 atm and 80 K, the two terms $1+\dfrac{V}{(V-b)}$ and $\dfrac{a}{VRT}$ are equal}
\opt{C}{At a pressure greater than 80 atm and 80 K, the term $\dfrac{V}{(V-b)}$ is greater an $\left(\dfrac{a}{VRT}+1\right)$}
\opt{D}{At 60 atm and 80 K, the term $\dfrac{V}{(V-b)}$ is smaller than $1+\dfrac{a}{VRT}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
